Is anyone else annoyed by the ambiguity of data measurement? Personally, I find it unacceptable. For example, the program nload measures global internet traffic. I know for a fact that by default it measures in base 2 (rounds to 1,024), but it's displayed units are SI (kBit/s, MBit/s, etc.) which rounds to 1,000. There are many more examples of this, all of which make me question whether something is actually 1 GiB or 1 GB.

Microsoft has decided not to be explicit about their units because they fear it'll cause confusion. Yes, it will cause confusion, but only for like six months. A small price to pay to do away with confusion all together.

And there'll be people who think that I'm being pretentious for insisting upon this. But there's a notable difference between 205 GiB and 205 GB (205 GB converts to ~191 GiB). I'm not comfortable with being unsure about that kind of gap.

Apparently there's a bit of a naming war that's been going on for quite some time. I'm arguing for the IEC standard. And while I prefer the IEC standard, I don't really care as long as we all decide on a standard and stick with it. At least be specific about what you're using.

For those of you who didn't even know this was a thing, I was in your shoes about six months ago. This might help.

All I know is that when I write programs, they'll follow the IEC standard. And I'll make it obvious that they follow the IEC standard. Because this is all just to stressful.
ambiguity of data measurement needs to stop

I agree. G, M, k, etc... all were assigned clear meaning a ling time ago when the SI system was developed. Coming in after the fact and usurping the terminology capriciously is stupid and arrogant, IMO.

I don't think you're being pretentious at all. You are, in fact, correct that those SI units represent 10^n.

Unfortunately, this seems to be more a problem of scientists being uncontrollably pedantic. I'm not going to lie, I've worked for many many years in a field that uses these units (as in bits, bytes, endianness, etc.) heavily, and for safety critical applications, no less. Not only have I only even heard the IEC prefixes mentioned in passing, but I have never, not once, been made aware an error that occurred due to the ambiguity in the prefix.

I think the crux of the issue here is that, in the real world, any computer scientist/engineer sufficiently qualified to work in their field will never make the mistake of thinking a kilobyte is 1000 bytes and not 1024 even though they know full well that kilo- is 10^3. Everyone just assumes kilo- is 1024 in the realm of computer science because it's so fundamental that these machines work in base 2 that forgetting it means forgetting computer science.

A Simple Proof From the Pattern-Matching Card Game Set Stuns Mathematicians

This is why we need to gamify more problems!

In a series of papers posted online in recent weeks, mathematicians have solved a problem about the pattern-matching card game Set that predates the game itself. The solution, whose simplicity has stunned mathematicians, is already leading to advances in other combinatorics problems.

So the solution to a tricky combinatorics problem came from a game strategy. Cool! There's math everywhere - especially in games.

Set has a simple goal: to find special triples called “sets” within a deck of 81 cards. Each card displays a different design with four attributes — color, shape, shading and number.

Simple enough. Sounds like a fun grab-the-matches type of card game.

Occasionally, there’s no set to be found among the 12 cards, so the players add three more cards. Even less frequently, there’s still no set to be found among the 15 cards. How big, one might wonder, is the largest collection of cards that contains no set?

Ah, and here we get to the hard math...

The answer is 20, ... But for mathematicians, this answer was just the beginning. After all, there’s nothing special about having designs with only four attributes ... imagine cards with more attributes (for instance, they could have additional images, or even play different sounds or have scratch-and-sniff smells). For every whole number n, there’s a version of Set with n attributes and 3n different cards.

Instead of solving the problem of Set, we solve the problem of every possible Set deck anyone can make.

To find an upper bound on the size of cap sets, mathematicians translate the game into geometry. ... The rules of the Set game translate neatly into the geometry of the resulting n-dimensional space: Every line in the space contains exactly three points, and three points form a set precisely when they lie on the same line. A cap set, therefore, is a collection of points that contains no complete lines.

Easy! It's like a Sudoku puzzle in 3 dimensions (or 4 dimensions, or n dimensions...)

The fact that the cap set problem finally yielded to such a simple technique is humbling, Ellenberg said. “It makes you wonder what else is actually easy.” ... “I think a lot of people will be thinking, ‘What can I do with this?’” Gowers said. ... on May 17, Gil Kalai ... point[ed] out that the cap set result can be used to prove the “Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture,” which concerns sets that overlap in a sunflower pattern.

This is why math and abstract sciences are so important. We've found a clever and simple way to solve what was once thought to be a tremendous problem - it's another piece of the huge multifaceted puzzle that we call the universe.

Maybe this will lead to new advances in cryptanalysis or industrial flow modeling. We don't know and that's what makes it so awesome!
